newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks plunge, spooked by dollar and Dow.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks plunge, spooked by dollar and Dow.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market tumbled on Monday, spooked by a sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Friday and the dollar's retreat against the yen.
The 225-share Nikkei dove 780.28 points or 3.98 percent to 18,824.18, racking up its largest point loss for calendar 1997.

"Investors have been worried about the recovery of the economy in recent sessions and then Wall Street plunged on Friday and the dollar weakened against the yen, both factors hurting investor sentiment further," Mikio Takada, Nikko Securities' general manager, said.
On Friday, the Dow slid 156.78 points to end at 8,031.22.
In late afternoon Tokyo the dollar was trading at around 115.50 yen, above its close of 114.80 yen in New York on Friday but well below the level of around 118 seen in Asia last week.

Some traders said the reversal for the dollar was merely a correction from its recent run-up to 119 yen. But dealers said there is also some concern about the high-flying U.S. stock market, which is in turn putting pressure on the dollar.
Brokers said the Dow's fall and the weak dollar hit Japanese blue chip exporters as a lower dollar against the yen reduces the value of profits earned abroad.
The loss of market players due to the summer holidays also increased volatility in the market, brokers said.
Market participants who had not gone on holiday waited for public and pension funds to come to the rescue but such help was slow to come, leading losses to snowball.

"It seems fund money allocations were concentrated at the beginning of the year and hopes of a cushion may not be realised and the market may take a while to recover." Keiko Kondo, a Merrill Lynch strategist, said. "Judging from how the economy looks, investors many not find much reason to invest in Japanese stocks now."

Market sources said in order for investors to regain their faith in the economy again, optimistic news to soothe nerves rattled by the recent glum industrial production data as well as signs of slackening sales in consumer goods was needed.
Brokers said the Nikkei average had crashed through various technical support levels on Monday and there were few factors on the horizon that would radically change its course.
They said the downside was being tentatively put at the lower end of 18,000.
News that Japan and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will provide a total of $4 billion each in loans to help ease Thailand's financial crisis had little direct impact on stocks.
But market sources said there was concern over Asian currencies and the possible knock-on effect on the dollar, and investors were watching for new developments.

"Overseas demand had been sort of a lifeline for Tokyo stocks but with the dollar weak and possibilities of turmoil in Asian economies, the outlook could be bleak," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell strategist Ryoji Musha.

A reshuffle in the top management of Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, which is involved in a racketeer payoff scandal that has also ensnared Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, was applauded by the market on hopes the new management would be able to help the brokerage recover from the scandal.
"I don't expect the shares to fall sharply from this level, as there are hopes Yamaichi may tie up with a foreign brokerage," said a trader at a second-tier brokerage.
Yamaichi's shares gained 30 yen, or 13.10 percent, to 259, making the broker the largest percentage gainer on the Tokyo bourse's first section.
